articles.title: Architecting for Velocity: How to Build an MVP Without Toxic Technical Debt
articles.summary: Practical principles for early-stage founders to ship fast while maintaining a clean, modular foundation that will not crumble after initial product-market fit.
articles.author: Jannatul (Founder & Lead Architect)

content.introduction: The biggest lie told to first-time founders is that speed requires sloppy code. In reality, bad code does not speed up the first month—it slows down the third month to a complete standstill.

sections.heading: 1. The Difference Between Pragmatism and Sloppiness
paragraphs: Pragmatism means choosing boring, battle-tested technologies with rich ecosystems. It means defining strict schema boundaries even if you only have three database tables.
Sloppiness, by contrast, is neglecting database migrations, skipping foreign key constraints, or relying on client-side authentication checks.
keyTakeaways: Always use a strongly typed language (TypeScript) across front and back.
Enforce database constraints early—schema integrity is nearly impossible to retrofit.

sections.heading: 2. Modular Architecture Over Microservices
paragraphs: Do not build microservices for a 5-person startup. A clean, modular monolith with clear domain boundaries gives you 10x the development velocity with zero distributed systems overhead.
When you organize code by feature domain rather than purely technical layer, refactoring or extracting a service later becomes trivial.
keyTakeaways: Monolith-first is the proven path for 99% of early SaaS products.
Invest in reliable CI/CD and automated typechecking from commit number one.

content.conclusion: Speed is a byproduct of clarity, not recklessness. When your data models and domain boundaries are explicit, shipping new features feels effortless.

articles.title: Beyond the Chatbot: Engineering Deterministic, Audit-Proof AI Workflows
articles.summary: Why probabilistic language models must be wrapped in deterministic validation layers before touching financial or operational enterprise systems.
articles.author: Jannatul (Founder & Lead Architect)

content.introduction: Prompt engineering is not software engineering. When building mission-critical business automation, you cannot accept an output that fails 5% of the time. Here is how to achieve 99%+ reliability with LLMs.

sections.heading: 1. Treat LLMs as Untrusted Parsing Engines
paragraphs: Never pass raw LLM text directly to database inserts or payment gateways. Every model output must pass through a strict schema validation boundary (such as Zod or Pydantic).
If the schema fails validation, trigger an automatic correction loop with the exact validation error fed back to the model.
keyTakeaways: Enforce strict JSON mode and typed response schemas.
Implement idempotent fallback routines for anomalous responses.

sections.heading: 2. Deterministic Mathematical Verification
paragraphs: LLMs are notoriously unreliable at arithmetic. When extracting financial invoices, do not ask the model to calculate subtotals—extract the atomic integers, and let deterministic JavaScript or Python verify the math.
If line items do not sum up to the invoice total, flag the discrepancy immediately for human review.
keyTakeaways: Never use LLMs for arithmetic—use code for math and models for perception.
Build a clear confidence score threshold for human-in-the-loop review.

content.conclusion: By treating language models as perception components inside a deterministic software harness, you get the flexibility of AI with the bulletproof reliability of traditional engineering.
